ordered_diagnoses: Spinal cord compression due to metastatic tumor

facts.raw_span: A 50-year-old man
no significant past medical history
1-week history of rapidly progressive gait disturbance
no back pain, fevers, night sweats, or weight loss
full strength throughout all extremities
decreased sensation from the T3 dermatome downward
four beats of clonus bilaterally
hyperreflexia in the lower extremities
profound ataxia, rendering him unable to walk more than a few steps
Contrast-enhanced MRI of the thoracic spine demonstrated a diffusely enhancing lesion centered at T1 with near-circumferential epidural extension causing severe cord compression
CT of the thoracic spine showed an expansile bony lesion of the T1 vertebral body with extension into the left pedicle and posterior elements
CT scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed no evidence of a primary malignancy

concepts.preferred_label: Spinal cord compression due to metastatic tumor
concepts.why: The patient has a diffusely enhancing lesion centered at T1 with near-circumferential epidural extension causing severe cord compression, and CT scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed no evidence of a primary malignancy, suggesting a metastatic tumor.

The patient has an expansile bony lesion of the T1 vertebral body with extension into the left pedicle and posterior elements, and CT scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed no evidence of a primary malignancy, suggesting a metastatic tumor.

The patient has decreased sensation from the T3 dermatome downward, four beats of clonus bilaterally, hyperreflexia in the lower extremities, and profound ataxia, rendering him unable to walk more than a few steps, suggesting a spinal cord injury.
The patient has an expansile bony lesion of the T1 vertebral body with extension into the left pedicle and posterior elements, suggesting a possible fracture.

rationales.F10: The presence of a diffusely enhancing lesion with near-circumferential epidural extension causing severe cord compression is highly suggestive of spinal cord compression due to a metastatic tumor or other lesion.
rationales.F11: The expansile bony lesion of the T1 vertebral body with extension into the left pedicle and posterior elements is highly indicative of a metastatic tumor or primary bone lesion.
rationales.F12: The absence of evidence of a primary malignancy in the chest, abdomen, and pelvis makes metastatic tumor less likely but does not rule it out entirely.
